rationale: B wins because it finds the sharper interpretive story hiding inside the same facts: "The AI agent's biggest savings didn't come from negotiating. They came from cancelling." A is strong, but its closest trend angle, "AI agents are moving into real finance work — with a human keeping the final sign-off," is the safer, flatter room-temperature version. B keeps the same viable data, vendor, governance, and pricing lanes, then adds a real contrarian lens a reporter could actually sell upstairs.
gaps_in_A: Missed the best contrarian angle: the beta savings mostly came from unused seats and auto-renewals, not glamorous negotiation. A leaves that buried inside proof questions instead of making it a story.
"AI agents are moving into real finance work — with a human keeping the final sign-off" is competent but generic; it sounds like a trend panel before it sounds like a piece.
"buyer-side pressure on vendors starts immediately" pushes past the evidence. The update proves Ramp can draft emails; it does not prove vendors have felt pressure yet.
"Companies are paying an average of $342,000 a year" risks blurring identified savings with realized savings, even though A correctly flags that weakness later.
gaps_in_B: "attacks revenue lines vendors have quietly relied on" is a little too certain. The update supports unused seats and auto-renewals; it does not prove vendor reliance or material revenue impact.
"The prevailing pitch for agentic AI is sophisticated work like negotiation" imports outside context. Fine as a column frame, but it needs support before it becomes a pitch claim.
"plans to charge enterprises later" over-compresses the fact pattern. The update says an enterprise tier with custom approval workflows is coming later this year, not that pricing is settled.
